en: Majjhima Nikāya 20:
The Discourse on the Stilling of Thought.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness should from time to time attend to five signs.
What are the five?

Here, monks, whatever sign a monk relies upon, and whatever sign he attends to, there arise in him evil, unwholesome thoughts associated with desire, associated with hatred, and associated with delusion. By that, monks—
The bhikkhu should attend to another sign, connected with the wholesome, instead of that [previous] sign.

As he attends to another sign, connected with the wholesome, instead of that sign, those evil unwholesome thoughts—whether accompanied by desire, accompanied by hatred, or accompanied by delusion—are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes internally settled, composed, unified, and concentrated.
“Just as, monks, a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice might drive out a large wedge with a small wedge,
pull it out, and turn it around; even so, monks, whatever sign a bhikkhu relies upon, and by attending to which sign,
unwholesome, unskillful thoughts arise— whether connected with desire, connected with ill will, or connected with delusion— by that [sign], monks,”
The bhikkhu should attend to another sign connected with the wholesome, different from that [previous] sign.

As he attends to another sign connected with the wholesome, different from that sign, those evil unwholesome thoughts—whether connected with desire, connected with hatred, or connected with delusion—are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes internally settled, composed, unified, and concentrated.
If, monks, while that bhikkhu is attending to another sign connected with the wholesome instead of that [original] sign,
evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with hatred, and connected with delusion still arise,
then that bhikkhu should examine the danger in those thoughts:
‘Such thoughts as these are unwholesome; such thoughts as these are blameworthy; such thoughts as these result in suffering.

As he examines the danger in those thoughts, whatever evil, unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled within himself, grows calm, becomes unified, and attains concentration.

“Just as, monks, a woman or a man— youthful, young, and fond of adornment— would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted by a snake’s carcass, a dog’s carcass, or a human carcass hanging from their neck; even so, monks,
if while that bhikkhu is attending to another sign connected with the wholesome, instead of that [previous] sign,
evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire and connected with hatred still arise.”
“Furthermore, monks, even when those thoughts are associated with delusion, that bhikkhu should examine the danger in those thoughts:
‘In this way these thoughts are unwholesome; in this way these thoughts are blameworthy; in this way these thoughts result in suffering.

As he examines the danger in those thoughts, whatever evil, unwholesome thoughts—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—are abandoned by him and come to an end.”
With their abandoning, his mind becomes internally settled, composed, unified, and concentrated. But if, monks,
while that bhikkhu is examining the danger in those thoughts,
evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with hatred, and connected with delusion still arise, then, monks, by him—
A bhikkhu should practice non-attention and non-mental engagement toward those thoughts.

As he practices non-attention and non-mental engagement toward those thoughts, whatever evil, unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled inwardly; it becomes stilled, unified, and concentrated.
"Just as, monks, a man with good eyesight, not wishing to see forms that have come into his field of vision,
would either close his eyes or look away elsewhere;
even so, monks, if that bhikkhu, while examining the danger in those very thoughts..."
Evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with hatred, and connected with delusion arise;
they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled within itself, grows calm, becomes unified, and attains concentration.
If, monks, while that bhikkhu is applying non-attention and non-mental engagement toward even those thoughts,
evil unwholesome thoughts associated with desire, associated with hatred, and associated with delusion still arise, then, monks,
that bhikkhu should attend to the settling of the mental formation of thought regarding those thoughts.

As he attends to the stilling of the mental formation of those thoughts, whatever evil, unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled within itself; it becomes stilled, unified, and concentrated.
Just as if, monks, a man were walking swiftly.
It might occur to him:
“Why am I walking so fast?
Suppose I were to walk slowly instead.”
He would walk slowly.
It would occur to him:
“Why indeed am I walking slowly?”
‘What if I were to remain? He would remain.
It would occur to him:
‘Am I standing? What if I were now to sit down?
He would then sit down.
It might occur to him:
“Why am I sitting? Suppose I were to lie down.”
He should lie down.
For in this way, monks, that man, having avoided each coarse posture, would adopt each subtle posture.
In the same way, monks, if that bhikkhu applies non-attention and non-mindfulness toward those thoughts as well, [they subside].
Evil, unwholesome thoughts—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—arise;
yet they are abandoned and they come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled and composed within itself; it becomes unified and concentrated.

If, monks, while that bhikkhu is attending to the stilling of the mental formation of those very thoughts, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with hatred, and connected with delusion still arise,
then, monks, that bhikkhu should clench his teeth, press his tongue against the palate, and restrain, suppress, and torment the mind with the mind.
When he clenches his teeth, presses his tongue against the palate, and with his mind forcefully restrains, suppresses, and oppresses the mind,
those evil, unwholesome thoughts— whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—
are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandoning, his mind becomes settled internally, grows calm, becomes unified, and attains concentration.
Just as if, monks, a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head, or by the neck, or by the shoulder, and restrain him, crush him, and torment him;
even so, monks, for that bhikkhu, there occurs the restraint of the mental formation of those very thoughts.
While he is attending to it, evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with ill will, and connected with delusion arise.

In that case, monks, that bhikkhu should clench his teeth, press his tongue against the palate, and restrain, suppress, and torment the mind with the mind. As he clenches his teeth, presses his tongue against the palate, and restrains, suppresses, and torments the mind with the mind— ... [the passage continues] ...
of him who clenches his teeth, presses his tongue against the palate, and restrains, suppresses, and torments the mind with the mind.
As he burns away [the mind], those evil, unwholesome thoughts associated with desire, associated with hatred,
and associated with delusion are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.
But when, monks, for a bhikkhu, by relying on a certain sign and attending to that sign, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, connected with hatred, and connected with delusion arise;
if he attends to another sign connected with the wholesome instead of that sign, those evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire... [arise no more].
Those thoughts associated with lust, associated with hatred, and associated with delusion are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.

As he examines the danger in those thoughts, whatever evil unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandoning, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.

As he applies non-attention and non-mindfulness toward those thoughts, whatever evil unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and vanish.
With their abandoning, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.

As he attends to the stilling of the mental formation of those very thoughts, whatever evil, unwholesome thoughts there may be—whether associated with desire, associated with hatred, or associated with delusion—they are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.
Pressing his teeth together and pressing his tongue against the palate, he restrains, suppresses, and subdues the mind with the mind.
As he burns away [the mind], those evil, unwholesome thoughts associated with desire, associated with hatred,
and associated with delusion are abandoned and come to an end.
With their abandonment, the mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within itself.
“Monks, this is called a monk who is a master over the pathways of thought.
Whatever thought he wishes to think, that thought he will think; whatever thought he does not wish to think, that thought he will not think.
He has cut off craving, turned away from the fetters, and through the complete penetration of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The monks were delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The *Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta*, the tenth, is finished.
The second chapter, the Chapter on the Lion’s Roar, is finished.
Its summary verse is:
The Shorter Lion’s Roar, the Hair-raising, and the Excellent.
The Mahācūḷadukkhakkhandha-anumānika-sutta;
the Khila, Pattha, Madhupiṇḍika, and Dvidhāvitakka;
and the section on the Five Signs.
